journeys.title: Abraham's Road
journeys.subtitle: From Ur of the Chaldees to a bought field in Hebron
journeys.essay: Abraham's road runs a thousand miles and more — Ur's canals to Haran's markets, then the long descent into Canaan, down to Egypt and back, and up one last hill he never asked to climb. The big story starts here, on foot. God's answer to Babel is not an empire but a walking family: one man told to leave country, kindred, and father's house for land he will never own, promised descendants he cannot count from a wife who cannot conceive. Every stage of the road tests that promise — famine, Pharaoh, quarreling herdsmen, decades of childlessness, finally the knife on Moriah. And every stage gets an altar, until the hill road of Canaan is staked out in field stones. Abraham dies owning one field and one cave, bought at full price. But the route he walked becomes the map of the whole Bible: his descendants go down to Egypt by his famine road, and come back up it toward the land he paced off on foot.

waypoints.placeNote: Great city of the Chaldees on the lower Euphrates, Abram's birthplace
waypoints.narration: The road begins in a city of brick and canal water, where the Euphrates crawls wide and brown past temple towers. Ur is old money and older gods; barges, ledgers, moon-worship on the high platform. Here Haran dies before his father Terah. Here Abram marries Sarai, who is barren. Then Terah gathers the household — Abram, Sarai, Lot — and walks away from all of it, upriver, bound for Canaan. The caravan leaves the ziggurat's shadow and takes the long river road north.
verses: And Haran died before his father Terah in the land of his nativity, in Ur of the Chaldees.
And Abram and Nahor took them wives: the name of Abram's wife was Sarai; and the name of Nahor's wife, Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah, and the father of Iscah.
But Sarai was barren; she had no child.

And Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son's son, and Sarai his daughter in law, his son Abram's wife; and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan; and they came unto Haran, and dwelt there.

waypoints.placeNote: Caravan crossroads town in upper Mesopotamia where Terah settled and died
waypoints.narration: Six hundred miles up the Euphrates corridor, past Mari and the caravan fords, the road bends west into Haran — a trading town on the Balikh, thick with sheep markets and the same moon god they left in Ur. Terah settles here, and here he dies. Then the word comes, plain as a drover's order: get out. Country, kindred, father's house — leave all three, for a land unnamed. Abram is seventy-five. He packs the tents, takes Sarai and Lot, and points the animals south.
verses: Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:
And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing:
And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.
So Abram departed, as the LORD had spoken unto him; and Lot went with him: and Abram was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran.

waypoints.placeNote: First camp in Canaan, in the pass between Ebal and Gerizim
waypoints.narration: Four hundred miles of it: down through Damascus country, along the rim of the Jordan trench, then up into the hills by the pass road. Shechem sits in the saddle between two mountains, and at the oak of Moreh the caravan finally stops. This is the land — occupied, Canaanite, not his. And here the LORD appears for the first time on the road: unto thy seed will I give this land. Abram answers the only way a wanderer can. He builds an altar of field stones.
verses: And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their substance that they had gathered, and the souls that they had gotten in Haran; and they went forth to go into the land of Canaan; and into the land of Canaan they came.
And Abram passed through the land unto the place of Sichem, unto the plain of Moreh. And the Canaanite was then in the land. plain: Heb. plains
And the LORD appeared unto Abram, and said, Unto thy seed will I give this land: and there builded he an altar unto the LORD, who appeared unto him.

waypoints.placeNote: Hill camp on the ridge road, Bethel to the west, Ai east
waypoints.narration: Twenty miles south along the watershed ridge, the spine road every drover in Canaan uses. Abram pitches his tent on a mountain with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east — high ground, thin soil, wide views over the land he has been promised and does not own. A second altar goes up here, and he calls on the name of the LORD; the road itself is becoming a string of altars. Then he strikes camp again and keeps moving, stage by stage, toward the dry south country.
verses: And he removed from thence unto a mountain on the east of Bethel, and pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west, and Hai on the east: and there he builded an altar unto the LORD, and called upon the name of the LORD.
And Abram journeyed, going on still toward the south. going...: Heb. in going and journeying

waypoints.placeNote: Nile kingdom of grain, Pharaoh's court, refuge in famine years
waypoints.narration: Famine empties the hills, so the road runs south and west — down through the Negev, across the desert track to Shur, into the green shock of the Nile delta. Egypt has grain when Canaan has dust. It also has Pharaoh. Afraid for his life, Abram passes Sarai off as his sister, and she is taken into Pharaoh's house while Abram is paid in sheep, oxen, and camels. It is a bad trade dressed as survival. Plagues fall on the palace, the lie surfaces, and the family is marched to the border.
verses: And there was a famine in the land: and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there; for the famine was grievous in the land.
And it came to pass, when he was come near to enter into Egypt, that he said unto Sarai his wife, Behold now, I know that thou art a fair woman to look upon:
Therefore it shall come to pass, when the Egyptians shall see thee, that they shall say, This is his wife: and they will kill me, but they will save thee alive.
Say, I pray thee, thou art my sister: that it may be well with me for thy sake; and my soul shall live because of thee.
And it came to pass, that, when Abram was come into Egypt, the Egyptians beheld the woman that she was very fair.
The princes also of Pharaoh saw her, and commended her before Pharaoh: and the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house.
And he entreated Abram well for her sake: and he had sheep, and oxen, and he asses, and menservants, and maidservants, and she asses, and camels.

waypoints.placeNote: Return to the first altar; where Abram and Lot part ways
waypoints.narration: Back up the long famine road, richer and more crowded than when they left. At Bethel the caravan stands again at the first altar, but the hill pasture cannot carry two households of this size. Herdsmen quarrel over wells and grazing while Canaanites watch. Abram, the elder, gives away the choice: left hand or right, take either. Lot lifts his eyes to the green Jordan plain — well watered, like Egypt, near Sodom — and takes it. They separate on the ridge, and the road forks for good.
verses: And Lot also, which went with Abram, had flocks, and herds, and tents.
And the land was not able to bear them, that they might dwell together: for their substance was great, so that they could not dwell together.
And there was a strife between the herdmen of Abram's cattle and the herdmen of Lot's cattle: and the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land.
And Abram said unto Lot, Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we be brethren. brethren: Heb. men brethren

Is not the whole land before thee? separate thyself, I pray thee, from me: if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if thou depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left.

And Lot lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, even as the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, as thou comest unto Zoar.
Then Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan; and Lot journeyed east: and they separated themselves the one from the other.

waypoints.placeNote: Oak grove above Hebron where Abram pitched his lasting camp
waypoints.narration: With Lot gone east, the LORD tells Abram to lift his own eyes — north, south, east, west — and then to walk the land like an owner pacing a field. So he walks it, thirty-five miles down the ridge to the oaks of Mamre at Hebron, high country of vineyards and old terebinths. Here he plants his tent for the long haul and builds a third altar. Shechem, Bethel, Hebron: the promise now has stakes driven at both ends and the middle of the hill road.
verses: And the LORD said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him, Lift up now thine eyes, and look from the place where thou art northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward:
For all the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed for ever.
And I will make thy seed as the dust of the earth: so that if a man can number the dust of the earth, then shall thy seed also be numbered.
Arise, walk through the land in the length of it and in the breadth of it; for I will give it unto thee.
Then Abram removed his tent, and came and dwelt in the plain of Mamre, which is in Hebron, and built there an altar unto the LORD. plain: Heb. plains

waypoints.placeNote: Open ground outside the Mamre camp, under a desert-clear night sky
waypoints.narration: A mile at most, out from the tents to open ground; tonight the journey stands still. Years have passed at Mamre and the promise still has no child to carry it — only Eliezer of Damascus, a steward penciled in as heir. In a vision the word comes: fear not, I am thy shield. Abram answers with the road-worn question, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless. Then God walks him out of the tent into the dark and tilts his head back. Count the stars, if you can. So shall thy seed be. Abram believes, and it is counted to him.
verses: After these things the word of the LORD came unto Abram in a vision, saying, Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward.
And Abram said, Lord GOD, what wilt thou give me, seeing I go childless, and the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus?
And Abram said, Behold, to me thou hast given no seed: and, lo, one born in my house is mine heir.
And, behold, the word of the LORD came unto him, saying, This shall not be thine heir; but he that shall come forth out of thine own bowels shall be thine heir.
And he brought him forth abroad, and said, Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be.
And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.

waypoints.placeNote: The mountain of the offering, three days north of the south country
waypoints.narration: The hardest road on this map is short and uphill. Three days out from the south country, Abraham lifts his eyes and sees the place afar off — a bare hill in the land of Moriah. He and Isaac climb alone, wood on the boy's back, fire and knife in the old man's hands. Altar, wood, cord, the knife raised — and then the voice out of heaven, and a ram caught by its horns in the thicket. Abraham names the hill The LORD Will Provide, and they walk down together.
verses: And they came to the place which God had told him of; and Abraham built an altar there, and laid the wood in order, and bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar upon the wood.
And Abraham stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son.
And the angel of the LORD called unto him out of heaven, and said, Abraham, Abraham: and he said, Here am I.
And he said, Lay not thine hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him: for now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me.

And Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and behold behind him a ram caught in a thicket by his horns: and Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering in the stead of his son.
And Abraham called the name of that place Jehovahjireh: as it is said to this day, In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen. Jehovahjireh: that is, The Lord will see, or, provide

waypoints.placeNote: Field and cave before Mamre, the first deeded ground in Canaan
waypoints.narration: The road comes back to Hebron carrying grief. Sarah dies at a hundred and twenty-seven, and Abraham — stranger and sojourner, he says — stands before the Hittites at the town gate needing one thing he has never owned: ground. Ephron talks like a giver and prices like a merchant. Four hundred shekels of silver, weighed out in front of witnesses. The field of Machpelah, its cave, its trees, made sure by contract. Abraham buries Sarah there. After a lifetime walking a promised land, this small deeded field is the first piece that is legally his.
verses: And Abraham hearkened unto Ephron; and Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.

And the field of Ephron, which was in Machpelah, which was before Mamre, the field, and the cave which was therein, and all the trees that were in the field, that were in all the borders round about, were made sure
Unto Abraham for a possession in the presence of the children of Heth, before all that went in at the gate of his city.
And after this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre: the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan.
And the field, and the cave that is therein, were made sure unto Abraham for a possession of a buryingplace by the sons of Heth.

journeys.title: The Exodus Road
journeys.subtitle: Out of Egypt by night, through the sea, to the mountain
journeys.essay: The Exodus is the Bible's master journey: a slave nation walks out of the strongest empire on earth and becomes a people on the road. It begins at midnight in Goshen, moves in forced-march stages to the edge of the sea, and passes through water that stands up in walls. After that the route turns south into hard country, and the road itself becomes the teacher — bitter water sweetened at Marah, an oasis of twelve springs at Elim, bread on the ground each morning in the wilderness of Sin, water struck from rock at Rephidim. Every stage strips Egypt out of the people a little more. The destination is not yet the promised land but a mountain: Sinai, wrapped in smoke and trumpet blast, where the freed slaves are given law and made a nation. Israel will retell this road forever — out of the house of bondage, through the sea, to the mountain of God.

waypoints.placeNote: Israel's district in the eastern Nile delta, land of Rameses
waypoints.narration: The road out of Egypt starts in the dark. Goshen is delta country — black soil, canals, brick pits where Israel has slaved for generations under the store-cities' quota. On this night the LORD passes through Egypt, and at midnight every firstborn in the land dies, from Pharaoh's house to the dungeon. A great cry goes up; there is not a house without its dead. Pharaoh summons Moses before sunrise: rise up, get out, take your flocks, and bless me also. The Egyptians push them out the door with silver in their hands.
verses: And it came to pass, that at midnight the LORD smote all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sat on his throne unto the firstborn of the captive that was in the dungeon; and all the firstborn of cattle. dungeon: Heb. house of the pit
And Pharaoh rose up in the night, he, and all his servants, and all the Egyptians; and there was a great cry in Egypt; for there was not a house where there was not one dead.
And he called for Moses and Aaron by night, and said, Rise up, and get you forth from among my people, both ye and the children of Israel; and go, serve the LORD, as ye have said.
Also take your flocks and your herds, as ye have said, and be gone; and bless me also.
And the Egyptians were urgent upon the people, that they might send them out of the land in haste; for they said, We be all dead men.

waypoints.placeNote: First camp east of Rameses, staging ground at the delta's edge
waypoints.narration: First stage, first count. From Rameses to Succoth is a short march, but it is the biggest column this road has ever carried — about six hundred thousand men on foot, plus children, plus a mixed multitude that decided to leave Egypt with them, plus herds beyond counting. At Succoth they stop and bake what they carried: unleavened cakes, dough with no time to rise, bread with the shape of haste pressed into it. Behind them the brick pits stand empty. Ahead, the edge of the wilderness.
verses: And the children of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand on foot that were men, beside children.
And a mixed multitude went up also with them; and flocks, and herds, even very much cattle. a mixed...: Heb. a great mixture

And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they brought forth out of Egypt, for it was not leavened; because they were thrust out of Egypt, and could not tarry, neither had they prepared for themselves any victual.

waypoints.placeNote: Camp on the edge of the wilderness where the pillar first led
waypoints.narration: Fifteen miles on, the green runs out. Etham sits at the edge of the wilderness, where delta mud gives way to gravel and the horizon flattens to nothing. God does not take them by the short coast road — that way lies Philistine war, and a people fresh from slavery might bolt back to Egypt. Instead a pillar of cloud goes up ahead of the column by day, and by night it burns as fire, so the road never goes dark. The pillar does not leave them. From here on, Israel follows the cloud, not the map.
verses: And they took their journey from Succoth, and encamped in Etham, in the edge of the wilderness.
And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night:
He took not away the pillar of the cloud by day, nor the pillar of fire by night, from before the people.

waypoints.placeNote: Camp by the sea, between Migdol and the water, facing Baal-zephon
waypoints.narration: The order comes to turn back and camp by the sea at Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the water — a dead end on purpose, a trap baited with a nation. Pharaoh takes the bait. Six hundred chosen chariots and all the cavalry of Egypt come down the road behind them, and Israel looks up to see dust and iron closing in, water at their backs. The people turn on Moses: were there no graves in Egypt. Fear talks like that. Moses answers with the only order left: stand still, and see.
verses: But the Egyptians pursued after them, all the horses and chariots of Pharaoh, and his horsemen, and his army, and overtook them encamping by the sea, beside Pihahiroth, before Baalzephon.
And when Pharaoh drew nigh, the children of Israel lifted up their eyes, and, behold, the Egyptians marched after them; and they were sore afraid: and the children of Israel cried out unto the LORD.
And they said unto Moses, Because there were no graves in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness? wherefore hast thou dealt thus with us, to carry us forth out of Egypt?

Is not this the word that we did tell thee in Egypt, saying, Let us alone, that we may serve the Egyptians? For it had been better for us to serve the Egyptians, than that we should die in the wilderness.

waypoints.placeNote: The crossing: walls of water, a dry seabed road between
waypoints.narration: Moses stretches his hand over the water and an east wind works all night, and by morning there is a road where no road can be — dry seabed, water standing in walls on the right hand and the left. The column crosses in the dark between two cliffs of sea. Egypt's chariots follow and the wheels come off; when morning appears the walls let go, and the strongest army on earth is unmade in the returning water. Israel stands on the far shore, out of the house of bondage. Behind them the sea is smooth, and the road home to slavery is gone.
verses: And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea; and the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.
And the children of Israel went into the midst of the sea upon the dry ground: and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left.
And the Egyptians pursued, and went in after them to the midst of the sea, even all Pharaoh's horses, his chariots, and his horsemen.
And it came to pass, that in the morning watch the LORD looked unto the host of the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and of the cloud, and troubled the host of the Egyptians,

And took off their chariot wheels, that they drave them heavily: so that the Egyptians said, Let us flee from the face of Israel; for the LORD fighteth for them against the Egyptians. that they...: or, and made them to go heavily
And the LORD said unto Moses, Stretch out thine hand over the sea, that the waters may come again upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots, and upon their horsemen.

And Moses stretched forth his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to his strength when the morning appeared; and the Egyptians fled against it; and the LORD overthrew the Egyptians in the midst of the sea. overthrew: Heb. shook off

waypoints.placeNote: Bitter spring three waterless days into the wilderness of Shur
waypoints.narration: Three days into the wilderness of Shur and the waterskins go slack. No wells, no shade, the herds bawling. Then a spring — and it is bitter, undrinkable, which is worse than no spring at all. They name the place Marah, bitterness, and the murmuring starts: what shall we drink. Moses cries out, and the LORD shows him a tree; cast into the waters, it turns them sweet. There God makes a statute for the road and proves the people. Freedom, it turns out, is learned one well at a time.
verses: So Moses brought Israel from the Red sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur; and they went three days in the wilderness, and found no water.
And when they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah. Marah: that is Bitterness
And the people murmured against Moses, saying, What shall we drink?

And he cried unto the LORD; and the LORD shewed him a tree, which when he had cast into the waters, the waters were made sweet: there he made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there he proved them,

waypoints.placeNote: Oasis of twelve springs and seventy palm trees
waypoints.narration: A short day's march past Marah the ground breaks into green: Elim, twelve fountains of water and seventy palm trees, the first good camp since Egypt. The itinerary in Numbers records it like a quartermaster — they removed from Marah, came to Elim, pitched there. One spring per tribe, shade enough for everyone, water that needs no miracle. The column rests, fills the skins, lets the animals graze. Not every stage of this road is a test; some are plain mercy. Then they strike the tents and move down toward the shore of the Red Sea again.
verses: And they removed from Marah, and came unto Elim: and in Elim were twelve fountains of water, and threescore and ten palm trees; and they pitched there.
And they removed from Elim, and encamped by the Red sea.

waypoints.placeNote: Barren stretch between Elim and Sinai where the manna began
waypoints.narration: Between Elim and Sinai the road crosses the wilderness of Sin, a month out of Egypt, and the food runs out. The people remember slavery as flesh pots and bread to the full, and say they would rather have died there. The answer comes on schedule: at evening, quail cover the camp; in the morning, when the dew lifts, the ground is scaled with something small, round, frost-white. Manna, they say — for they wist not what it was. This is the bread the LORD has given you, says Moses, and it will fall every morning of the road ahead.
verses: And it came to pass, that at even the quails came up, and covered the camp: and in the morning the dew lay round about the host.
And when the dew that lay was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground.

And when the children of Israel saw it, they said one to another, It is manna: for they wist not what it was. And Moses said unto them, This is the bread which the LORD hath given you to eat. It is...: or, What is this? or, It is a portion

waypoints.placeNote: Dry camp below Horeb; water from the struck rock
waypoints.narration: Rephidim is a dry camp in high desert, granite ridges closing in, and there is no water at all. The murmuring turns dangerous — Moses tells the LORD the people are almost ready to stone him. The order: go ahead of them with the elders, take the rod that struck the Nile, and strike the rock in Horeb. Water comes out of stone in front of witnesses. They name the place Massah and Meribah, testing and quarreling, because here the question was asked out loud: is the LORD among us, or not. The road's answer stands wet on the rock.
verses: And the people thirsted there for water; and the people murmured against Moses, and said, Wherefore is this that thou hast brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our cattle with thirst?
And Moses cried unto the LORD, saying, What shall I do unto this people? they be almost ready to stone me.
And the LORD said unto Moses, Go on before the people, and take with thee of the elders of Israel; and thy rod, wherewith thou smotest the river, take in thine hand, and go.

Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it, that the people may drink. And Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel.

waypoints.placeNote: The mountain of God, where Israel camped and received the law
waypoints.narration: The road ends at a wall of granite. Israel camps on the plain before Sinai, and on the third morning the mountain goes off like a storm and a furnace at once — thunder, lightning, a cloud clamped on the summit, a trumpet blast that grows louder instead of fading. The whole mount smokes and shakes; the people tremble at the foot of it. Moses climbs into the cloud alone. Out of that fire come the words that turn a freed mob into a nation. Fifty days after the brick pits, Israel stands at the mountain of God, and the wandering has a covenant.
verses: And it came to pass on the third day in the morning, that there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud upon the mount, and the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud; so that all the people that was in the camp trembled.
And Moses brought forth the people out of the camp to meet with God; and they stood at the nether part of the mount.
And mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the LORD descended upon it in fire: and the smoke thereof ascended as the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mount quaked greatly.
And when the voice of the trumpet sounded long, and waxed louder and louder, Moses spake, and God answered him by a voice.
And the LORD came down upon mount Sinai, on the top of the mount: and the LORD called Moses up to the top of the mount; and Moses went up.

journeys.title: The Long Way Round
journeys.subtitle: Thirty-eight years from Sinai to the river's edge
journeys.essay: Eleven days' walk separates Sinai from the southern gate of Canaan. Israel takes thirty-eight years. The journey begins in order, ranks and standards moving under the cloud, and unravels almost at once: fire at Taberah, graves at Kibroth-hattaavah, leprosy at Hazeroth. At Kadesh the spies bring back grapes and fear together, and fear wins. The generation that saw the Red Sea open chooses to die in the desert rather than fight for the land, and gets its wish one funeral at a time. What follows is the long loop — south past Edom, around Moab, up the far side of the Dead Sea — while the children grow into soldiers. The crossing of the little brook Zered closes the account of the old generation. By the Arnon, Israel is conquering rather than wandering. The road ends where it can finally see its destination: Moses on Pisgah, the land spread out before him, the river between.

waypoints.placeNote: The mountain of the law; Israel's camp for nearly a year
waypoints.narration: For nearly a year the camp has lain under the granite wall of Sinai, long enough for the tents to wear paths between them. On the twentieth day of the second month the cloud lifts off the tabernacle, and the whole nation folds itself up: tent pegs pulled, ark shouldered, herds gathered in from the wadis. Ahead lies the wilderness of Paran, a plain of flint and drift sand. The people move out in ranks by their standards, the way north stretching pale in the morning light. Nobody guesses the road will take thirty-eight more years.
verses: And it came to pass on the twentieth day of the second month, in the second year, that the cloud was taken up from off the tabernacle of the testimony.
And the children of Israel took their journeys out of the wilderness of Sinai; and the cloud rested in the wilderness of Paran.
And they first took their journey according to the commandment of the LORD by the hand of Moses.

waypoints.placeNote: A burned camp three days out; the name means Burning
waypoints.narration: Three days out from the mountain and the shine has already worn off the road. The marching order drags, water is measured, the wind carries grit into everything. Complaint runs through the camp like a low fever, and at the outskirts fire breaks out — not cook-fire, but fire of the LORD, eating through the outlying tents. The people cry to Moses; Moses prays; the fire sinks. They name the place Taberah, Burning, and it keeps the name after the ashes cool. The column moves on, quieter now, watching the cloud.
verses: And when the people complained, it displeased the LORD: and the LORD heard it; and his anger was kindled; and the fire of the LORD burnt among them, and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp. complained: or, were as it were complainers it displeased: Heb. it was evil in the ears of
And the people cried unto Moses; and when Moses prayed unto the LORD, the fire was quenched. was...: Heb. sunk
And he called the name of the place Taberah: because the fire of the LORD burnt among them. Taberah: that is, A burning

waypoints.placeNote: The graves of craving, where the quail eaters were buried
waypoints.narration: The craving starts with the rabble and spreads: fish, cucumbers, melons, the food of Egypt remembered better than Egypt deserved. Then a wind comes off the sea and lays quail around the camp a day's journey in every direction, drifted two cubits deep. All that day and night and the next day the people gather them, spreading carcasses on the rocks, ten homers to the least gatherer. The meat is still between their teeth when the plague strikes. They dig graves in the gravel — Kibroth-hattaavah, the graves of craving — and the road out of camp runs straight between the mounds.
verses: And there went forth a wind from the LORD, and brought quails from the sea, and let them fall by the camp, as it were a day's journey on this side, and as it were a day's journey on the other side, round about the camp, and as it were two cubits high upon the face of the earth. as it were a day's...: Heb. as it were the way of a day

And the people stood up all that day, and all that night, and all the next day, and they gathered the quails: he that gathered least gathered ten homers: and they spread them all abroad for themselves round about the camp.
And while the flesh was yet between their teeth, ere it was chewed, the wrath of the LORD was kindled against the people, and the LORD smote the people with a very great plague.
And he called the name of that place Kibrothhattaavah: because there they buried the people that lusted. Kibrothhattaavah: that is, The graves of lust

waypoints.placeNote: A well-stop northeast of Sinai where Miriam was struck leprous
waypoints.narration: A short march northeast brings the camp to Hazeroth, a huddle of enclosures near thin wells. Here the trouble comes from inside the family: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses, measuring their own gift of prophecy against his. The LORD calls all three out to the tabernacle door and comes down in the pillar of cloud to answer — with Moses I speak mouth to mouth. When the cloud lifts, Miriam stands leprous, white as snow. Seven days the whole camp sits still while she is shut outside it, and no one moves a tent peg until she is brought in again.
verses: And Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married: for he had married an Ethiopian woman. Ethiopian: or, Cushite married: Heb. taken
And they said, Hath the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us? And the LORD heard it.
(Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth.)
And the LORD spake suddenly unto Moses, and unto Aaron, and unto Miriam, Come out ye three unto the tabernacle of the congregation. And they three came out.
And the LORD came down in the pillar of the cloud, and stood in the door of the tabernacle, and called Aaron and Miriam: and they both came forth.
And he said, Hear now my words: If there be a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream.
My servant Moses is not so, who is faithful in all mine house.
With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the LORD shall he behold: wherefore then were ye not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?
And the anger of the LORD was kindled against them; and he departed.
And the cloud departed from off the tabernacle; and, behold, Miriam became leprous, white as snow: and Aaron looked upon Miriam, and, behold, she was leprous.

waypoints.placeNote: Spring oasis on Canaan's southern rim; the spies' turning point
waypoints.narration: North across the wilderness of Paran, long dry stages between water, to the springs of Kadesh on the southern rim of Canaan. The land itself is close enough to smell. Twelve men went up from here; after forty days they come back down the wadi carrying a cluster of grapes on a pole between two of them. The report splits the camp: milk and honey, say all twelve, but ten see only walled cities and the sons of Anak, and call themselves grasshoppers. Caleb stands up alone with Joshua. The people choose the fear. The door north swings shut for a generation.
verses: And they went and came to Moses, and to Aaron, and to all the congregation of the children of Israel, unto the wilderness of Paran, to Kadesh; and brought back word unto them, and unto all the congregation, and shewed them the fruit of the land.
And they told him, and said, We came unto the land whither thou sentest us, and surely it floweth with milk and honey; and this is the fruit of it.
Nevertheless the people be strong that dwell in the land, and the cities are walled, and very great: and moreover we saw the children of Anak there.
The Amalekites dwell in the land of the south: and the Hittites, and the Jebusites, and the Amorites, dwell in the mountains: and the Canaanites dwell by the sea, and by the coast of Jordan.
And Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it.
But the men that went up with him said, We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we.

And they brought up an evil report of the land which they had searched unto the children of Israel, saying, The land, through which we have gone to search it, is a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof; and all the people that we saw in it are men of a great stature. men...: Heb. men of statures
And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.

waypoints.placeNote: Bare peak on Edom's border where Aaron died
waypoints.narration: The years at Kadesh end and the column swings southeast along the border of Edom, whose king has refused Israel the road. Mount Hor stands up out of the desert, bare and red. Aaron climbs it wearing the garments of the high priest and comes to the summit with Moses and Eleazar; there the garments pass from father to son, piece by piece. Aaron dies on the top of the mountain, in sight of the whole congregation on the plain below. Thirty days Israel mourns at the mountain's foot before anyone takes up the road again.
verses: And the children of Israel, even the whole congregation, journeyed from Kadesh, and came unto mount Hor.
And the LORD spake unto Moses and Aaron in mount Hor, by the coast of the land of Edom, saying,

Aaron shall be gathered unto his people: for he shall not enter into the land which I have given unto the children of Israel, because ye rebelled against my word at the water of Meribah. word: Heb. mouth
Take Aaron and Eleazar his son, and bring them up unto mount Hor:
And strip Aaron of his garments, and put them upon Eleazar his son: and Aaron shall be gathered unto his people, and shall die there.
And Moses did as the LORD commanded: and they went up into mount Hor in the sight of all the congregation.
And Moses stripped Aaron of his garments, and put them upon Eleazar his son; and Aaron died there in the top of the mount: and Moses and Eleazar came down from the mount.
And when all the congregation saw that Aaron was dead, they mourned for Aaron thirty days, even all the house of Israel.

waypoints.placeNote: Desert stream marking the end of thirty-eight wasted years
waypoints.narration: The long way around Edom: south almost to the gulf, then east and north again through country with no shade worth the name. This is the road that uses up the last of the old generation, the men of war who marched out of Egypt. At the bottom of a deep valley runs the brook Zered, thin water over stones. Thirty-eight years after Kadesh-barnea, the people cross it — a few minutes of wading. On the far bank stands a new nation, desert-born, and the word from God is plain at last: rise up, and get you over.
verses: Now rise up, said I, and get you over the brook Zered. And we went over the brook Zered. brook: or, valley

And the space in which we came from Kadeshbarnea, until we were come over the brook Zered, was thirty and eight years; until all the generation of the men of war were wasted out from among the host, as the LORD sware unto them. brook: or, valley
For indeed the hand of the LORD was against them, to destroy them from among the host, until they were consumed.

waypoints.placeNote: Gorge river on Moab's north border, edge of Amorite country
waypoints.narration: North along the edge of Moab the tableland begins to break into gorges, and the Arnon is the great one — a canyon cut deep through the plateau, the border between Moab and the Amorites. The camps hop from wadi to wadi, well to well, and the people pitch on the far side of the river. The old war songs remember this stretch: the brooks of Arnon, the stream that runs down to the dwelling of Ar. From here the road stops skirting other nations' countries. Sihon's kingdom ahead will have to be gone through, not around.
verses: From thence they removed, and pitched on the other side of Arnon, which is in the wilderness that cometh out of the coasts of the Amorites: for Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites.
Wherefore it is said in the book of the wars of the LORD, What he did in the Red sea, and in the brooks of Arnon, What...: or, Vaheb in Suphah
And at the stream of the brooks that goeth down to the dwelling of Ar, and lieth upon the border of Moab. lieth: Heb. leaneth

waypoints.placeNote: Pisgah's summit opposite Jericho; Moses' last lookout
waypoints.narration: The last camp spreads across the plains of Moab, opposite Jericho, close enough to see the green line of the Jordan. Moses climbs alone from the plain to the top of Pisgah on Mount Nebo. From the summit the whole land opens: Gilead to Dan, the hill country of Ephraim and Judah, the southern Negev, the palms of Jericho, out to the utmost sea. He sees all of it and crosses none of it. Moses dies there in the land of Moab, and God buries him in a valley no man has ever found. Below, the people face the river.
verses: And Moses went up from the plains of Moab unto the mountain of Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, that is over against Jericho. And the LORD shewed him all the land of Gilead, unto Dan, Pisgah: or, the hill
And all Naphtali, and the land of Ephraim, and Manasseh, and all the land of Judah, unto the utmost sea,
And the south, and the plain of the valley of Jericho, the city of palm trees, unto Zoar.

And the LORD said unto him, This is the land which I sware unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, saying, I will give it unto thy seed: I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither.
So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD.
And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.

journeys.title: Into the Land
journeys.subtitle: Jordan to Shiloh: the campaigns that won Canaan
journeys.essay: Forty years after Egypt, Israel stands on the east bank of the Jordan with a new commander and an old promise. The conquest is quick where the wandering was slow: the river stops, Jericho's wall falls, and the war divides into three campaigns — the center at Ai and Shechem, the south with the long day at Gibeon, the north ending in the burning of Hazor. Joshua's route is a soldier's route, from camp to siege to forced night march. Yet underneath the fighting runs a quieter thread of stones: twelve hauled out of the riverbed at Gilgal, an altar of unhewn rock on Ebal with the whole law read aloud between two mountains, each pile set up so a child on the road could ask what happened here. The journey ends not on a battlefield but at Shiloh, where the tabernacle that crossed the desert is finally set down and the land is divided by lot.

waypoints.placeNote: Acacia camp on Moab's plains, Israel's last stop east of Jordan
waypoints.narration: The camp at Shittim sits among acacia groves on the plains of Moab, the Jordan a green trench to the west and Jericho's palms visible beyond it. Moses is a month buried; the command now runs through Joshua. Officers pass down the tent rows with a plain order: prepare victuals, for within three days you cross this Jordan. The eastern tribes — Reuben, Gad, half Manasseh — are held to their old bargain: their families and cattle stay, their fighting men go over armed at the front of their brothers. The whole camp becomes an army sorting itself out. The river is at flood.
verses: Then Joshua commanded the officers of the people, saying,

Pass through the host, and command the people, saying, Prepare you victuals; for within three days ye shall pass over this Jordan, to go in to possess the land, which the LORD your God giveth you to possess it.
And to the Reubenites, and to the Gadites, and to half the tribe of Manasseh, spake Joshua, saying,
Remember the word which Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, saying, The LORD your God hath given you rest, and hath given you this land.

Your wives, your little ones, and your cattle, shall remain in the land which Moses gave you on this side Jordan; but ye shall pass before your brethren armed, all the mighty men of valour, and help them; armed: Heb. marshalled by five

Until the LORD have given your brethren rest, as he hath given you, and they also have possessed the land which the LORD your God giveth them: then ye shall return unto the land of your possession, and enjoy it, which Moses the LORD'S servant gave you on this side Jordan toward the sunrising.

waypoints.placeNote: Flood-stage ford opposite Jericho where the river stood in a heap
waypoints.narration: It is harvest season and the Jordan runs over all its banks, wide, brown, and fast. The ark goes first, a long gap kept between it and the people. The moment the priests' feet dip in the brim, the water fails: far upstream at the city Adam the current stands and rises up in a heap, and everything below drains away toward the salt sea. The priests stand firm on dry ground in mid-channel while the whole nation files past, right against Jericho. Twelve men each shoulder a stone out of the riverbed on the way through.
verses: And it came to pass, when the people removed from their tents, to pass over Jordan, and the priests bearing the ark of the covenant before the people;

And as they that bare the ark were come unto Jordan, and the feet of the priests that bare the ark were dipped in the brim of the water, (for Jordan overfloweth all his banks all the time of harvest,)

That the waters which came down from above stood and rose up upon an heap very far from the city Adam, that is beside Zaretan: and those that came down toward the sea of the plain, even the salt sea, failed, and were cut off: and the people passed over right against Jericho.

And the priests that bare the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firm on dry ground in the midst of Jordan, and all the Israelites passed over on dry ground, until all the people were passed clean over Jordan.

waypoints.placeNote: First camp in Canaan, ring of twelve stones from the riverbed
waypoints.narration: The people come up out of Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and pitch at Gilgal, on the east border of Jericho — the first camp on the west bank. Joshua sets up the twelve stones carried out of the riverbed, a rough ring standing in the plain. The purpose is stated outright: when your children ask their fathers what these stones mean, tell them Israel came over this Jordan on dry land. Gilgal becomes the base camp of the whole war. For years the army will march out from this ring of stones and return to it.
verses: And the people came up out of Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and encamped in Gilgal, in the east border of Jericho.
And those twelve stones, which they took out of Jordan, did Joshua pitch in Gilgal.
And he spake unto the children of Israel, saying, When your children shall ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean these stones? in time...: Heb. to morrow
Then ye shall let your children know, saying, Israel came over this Jordan on dry land.
For the LORD your God dried up the waters of Jordan from before you, until ye were passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red sea, which he dried up from before us, until we were gone over:
That all the people of the earth might know the hand of the LORD, that it is mighty: that ye might fear the LORD your God for ever. for ever: Heb. all days

waypoints.placeNote: Walled oasis city of palms, first fortress of Canaan to fall
waypoints.narration: Two miles from camp, Jericho sits shut up behind its wall, gates barred, none going out and none coming in. The tactic makes no military sense: once around the city each day — armed men, seven priests with rams' horns, the ark — and no shouting. Six days the pattern holds. On the seventh they rise at dawn and circle seven times, and at the seventh pass the horns blow long and Joshua gives the word. The shout goes up, the wall goes down flat, and the army climbs straight in over the rubble, every man from where he stands. Only Rahab's house is left standing.
verses: And it came to pass on the seventh day, that they rose early about the dawning of the day, and compassed the city after the same manner seven times: only on that day they compassed the city seven times.
And it came to pass at the seventh time, when the priests blew with the trumpets, Joshua said unto the people, Shout; for the LORD hath given you the city.

And the city shall be accursed, even it, and all that are therein, to the LORD: only Rahab the harlot shall live, she and all that are with her in the house, because she hid the messengers that we sent. accursed: or, devoted

And ye, in any wise keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest ye make yourselves accursed, when ye take of the accursed thing, and make the camp of Israel a curse, and trouble it. accursed: or, devoted a curse: or, devoted
But all the silver, and gold, and vessels of brass and iron, are consecrated unto the LORD: they shall come into the treasury of the LORD. consecrated: Heb. holiness

So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets: and it came to pass, when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city. flat: Heb. under it

waypoints.placeNote: Hill town above a ravine, taken by ambush after a first defeat
waypoints.narration: The road climbs west out of the Jordan trench into the hill country, toward the small town of Ai beside Bethaven. The first assault ended in a rout and thirty-six dead on the descent. This time Joshua sets an ambush behind the town by night and baits the garrison out with a false retreat. At the stretch of his spear the ambush rises, takes the emptied town, and fires it. The men of Ai turn to see their own smoke standing against the sky, and find the fleeing Israelites turned around and coming back. Caught between the two, the garrison is destroyed.
verses: And the LORD said unto Joshua, Stretch out the spear that is in thy hand toward Ai; for I will give it into thine hand. And Joshua stretched out the spear that he had in his hand toward the city.
And the ambush arose quickly out of their place, and they ran as soon as he had stretched out his hand: and they entered into the city, and took it, and hasted and set the city on fire.

And when the men of Ai looked behind them, they saw, and, behold, the smoke of the city ascended up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that way: and the people that fled to the wilderness turned back upon the pursuers. power: Heb. hand
And when Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had taken the city, and that the smoke of the city ascended, then they turned again, and slew the men of Ai.

waypoints.placeNote: Bald northern mountain over Shechem, mount of the curses
waypoints.narration: A long march north through the spine of the hills brings all Israel to the valley of Shechem, where Ebal and Gerizim stand facing each other across the pass. On Ebal, the bare northern mountain, Joshua builds an altar of whole stones over which no iron has been lifted, and burnt offerings go up from it. He writes a copy of the law of Moses on stones, then reads it out — all of it, the blessings and the cursings — half the tribes ranged on one slope and half on the other, the ark in the valley between. The war pauses for a public reading.
verses: Then Joshua built an altar unto the LORD God of Israel in mount Ebal,

As Moses the servant of the LORD commanded the children of Israel, as it is written in the book of the law of Moses, an altar of whole stones, over which no man hath lift up any iron: and they offered thereon burnt offerings unto the LORD, and sacrificed peace offerings.
And he wrote there upon the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he wrote in the presence of the children of Israel.

And all Israel, and their elders, and officers, and their judges, stood on this side the ark and on that side before the priests the Levites, which bare the ark of the covenant of the LORD, as well the stranger, as he that was born among them; half of them over against mount Gerizim, and half of them over against mount Ebal; as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded before, that they should bless the people of Israel.
And afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessings and cursings, according to all that is written in the book of the law.

There was not a word of all that Moses commanded, which Joshua read not before all the congregation of Israel, with the women, and the little ones, and the strangers that were conversant among them. were...: Heb. walked

waypoints.placeNote: Great Hivite city northwest of Jerusalem, spared by treaty
waypoints.narration: Gibeon bought its peace by trick — patched sandals, dry bread, a tale of a far country — and the treaty holds anyway. When five Amorite kings besiege the city for defecting, its runners reach Gilgal by night, and Joshua marches his army up from the Jordan floor in the dark, thousands of feet of climb, to fall on the siege lines at dawn. The rout pours down the pass toward Beth-horon, hailstones killing more than the sword. Over the fighting Joshua speaks to the sky, and the sun stands still upon Gibeon, the moon in the valley of Ajalon, until the work is finished.
verses: Then spake Joshua to the LORD in the day when the LORD delivered up the Amorites before the children of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon. stand...: Heb. be silent

And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. Is not this written in the book of Jasher? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day. Jasher: or, the upright?
And there was no day like that before it or after it, that the LORD hearkened unto the voice of a man: for the LORD fought for Israel.

waypoints.placeNote: Head city of the northern kingdoms, by the waters of Merom
waypoints.narration: The northern kings mass at the waters of Merom with horses and chariots, an army like the sand for multitude, and the road runs nearly a hundred miles north from Gilgal to meet them. Joshua strikes suddenly by the water and the coalition breaks, chased west to great Zidon and east into the valleys. The horses are lamed and the chariots burned, as commanded. Then he turns back to Hazor, beforetime the head of all those kingdoms, and takes it: king and city put to the sword, and Hazor itself burned — the only northern city Israel gives to the fire.
verses: And the LORD said unto Joshua, Be not afraid because of them: for to morrow about this time will I deliver them up all slain before Israel: thou shalt hough their horses, and burn their chariots with fire.
So Joshua came, and all the people of war with him, against them by the waters of Merom suddenly; and they fell upon them.

And the LORD delivered them into the hand of Israel, who smote them, and chased them unto great Zidon, and unto Misrephothmaim, and unto the valley of Mizpeh eastward; and they smote them, until they left them none remaining. great Zidon: or, Zidonrabbah Misrephothmaim: or, Salt pits: Heb. Burnings of waters
And Joshua did unto them as the LORD bade him: he houghed their horses, and burnt their chariots with fire.
And Joshua at that time turned back, and took Hazor, and smote the king thereof with the sword: for Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms.
And they smote all the souls that were therein with the edge of the sword, utterly destroying them: there was not any left to breathe: and he burnt Hazor with fire. any...: Heb. any breath

waypoints.placeNote: Hill-country town where the tabernacle rested and the land was divided
waypoints.narration: The war cools into settlement, and the whole congregation gathers at Shiloh, a quiet bowl in the hills of Ephraim north of Bethel. Here the tabernacle that crossed the Red Sea and forty years of desert is finally set up on ground that belongs to it. Seven tribes still wait for their inheritance, and Joshua prods them plainly: how long are you slack to go possess the land? Surveyors go out, three men to a tribe, to walk the country and describe it, and the lots are drawn before the LORD. The ark will rest at Shiloh for three hundred years.
verses: And the whole congregation of the children of Israel assembled together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of the congregation there. And the land was subdued before them.
And there remained among the children of Israel seven tribes, which had not yet received their inheritance.
And Joshua said unto the children of Israel, How long are ye slack to go to possess the land, which the LORD God of your fathers hath given you?

Give out from among you three men for each tribe: and I will send them, and they shall rise, and go through the land, and describe it according to the inheritance of them; and they shall come again to me.

journeys.title: David's Flight
journeys.subtitle: Seven hunted years through the hills of Judah, cave to crown
journeys.essay: Samuel has already poured the oil, but the throne belongs to Saul, and Saul has a javelin. What follows is seven years of running: down off the Benjamin ridge, through the priests' town, into enemy Gath, then out along the caves and wadis of southern Judah. This road is where the king was made. David gathers broken men at Adullam and turns them into a company. He spares the king who hunts him because the LORD's anointed is not his to kill. He loses everything at Ziklag and finds his footing in God alone. Many of the psalms carry these place-names in their titles: the cave, the wilderness of Ziph, the day Saul walked into the cave at En-gedi. When the crown finally comes at Hebron, it comes to a man the desert has already taught to wait for God. The flight is not a detour from the kingdom; it is the forge of it.

waypoints.placeNote: Saul's fortress town on the Benjamin ridge, three miles north of Jerusalem
waypoints.narration: Saul's town sits on its ridge, and the road climbs to it through vineyards and stone terraces. Inside the house the king sits with a javelin across his knees while David plays the harp. The spear splits the wall where David's head had been. That night Michal ropes her husband down through a window and the hunted years begin. Stand under the sill and look south: the whole length of Judah waits in the dark, and every mile of it is about to learn David's name.
verses: And the evil spirit from the LORD was upon Saul, as he sat in his house with his javelin in his hand: and David played with his hand.
And Saul sought to smite David even to the wall with the javelin; but he slipped away out of Saul's presence, and he smote the javelin into the wall: and David fled, and escaped that night.

Saul also sent messengers unto David's house, to watch him, and to slay him in the morning: and Michal David's wife told him, saying, If thou save not thy life to night, to morrow thou shalt be slain.
So Michal let David down through a window: and he went, and fled, and escaped.

waypoints.placeNote: The priests' town on the ridge, keeping the shewbread and Goliath's sword
waypoints.narration: An hour's walk south, on the shoulder of the ridge overlooking Jerusalem, stands the town of the priests. David arrives alone, unarmed, hungry, and spins Ahimelech a story about the king's business. There is no bread but the shewbread, no weapon but the sword of Goliath wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. David takes both. By the doorway stands Doeg the Edomite, watching, and his silence will one day cost this town every priest in it. The road out drops west, fast, toward country where Saul's writ does not run.
verses: Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest: and Ahimelech was afraid at the meeting of David, and said unto him, Why art thou alone, and no man with thee? Ahimelech: also called Ahiah

And David said unto Ahimelech the priest, The king hath commanded me a business, and hath said unto me, Let no man know any thing of the business whereabout I send thee, and what I have commanded thee: and I have appointed my servants to such and such a place.
Now therefore what is under thine hand? give me five loaves of bread in mine hand, or what there is present. present: Heb. found
And the priest answered David, and said, There is no common bread under mine hand, but there is hallowed bread; if the young men have kept themselves at least from women.

And David answered the priest, and said unto him, Of a truth women have been kept from us about these three days, since I came out, and the vessels of the young men are holy, and the bread is in a manner common, yea, though it were sanctified this day in the vessel. yea...: or, especially when this day there is other sanctified in the vessel
So the priest gave him hallowed bread: for there was no bread there but the shewbread, that was taken from before the LORD, to put hot bread in the day when it was taken away.
Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the LORD; and his name was Doeg, an Edomite, the chiefest of the herdmen that belonged to Saul.
And David said unto Ahimelech, And is there not here under thine hand spear or sword? for I have neither brought my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king's business required haste.

And the priest said, The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom thou slewest in the valley of Elah, behold, it is here wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod: if thou wilt take that, take it: for there is no other save that here. And David said, There is none like that; give it me.

waypoints.placeNote: Goliath's home city, out on the Philistine plain
waypoints.narration: Twenty-five miles down out of the hills, the road levels onto the Philistine plain and runs into Gath, the home city of Goliath. David walks in carrying Goliath's own sword, and the servants of Achish know his face from the victory songs. Cornered, he lets his spittle run into his beard and claws marks on the doors of the gate. The king of Gath waves the madman away, and it works. David leaves the enemy's capital alive, but there is nowhere lower for the anointed of Israel to stand.
verses: And David arose, and fled that day for fear of Saul, and went to Achish the king of Gath.

And the servants of Achish said unto him, Is not this David the king of the land? did they not sing one to another of him in dances, saying, Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands?
And David laid up these words in his heart, and was sore afraid of Achish the king of Gath.
And he changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard. scrabbled: or, made marks
Then said Achish unto his servants, Lo, ye see the man is mad: wherefore then have ye brought him to me? is mad: or, playeth the mad man
Have I need of mad men, that ye have brought this fellow to play the mad man in my presence? shall this fellow come into my house?

waypoints.placeNote: A limestone cave in the low hills above the valley of Elah
waypoints.narration: Back up the valley of Elah, where the hills first buckle out of the plain, a limestone cave opens above the terraces. David holes up here, and word travels. His brothers come down from Bethlehem. Then the others come: men in debt, men in distress, men with nothing left to lose, about four hundred of them. In the cool dark of Adullam an outlaw becomes a captain, and the ragged company that will one day carry a kingdom starts learning to answer to his voice.
verses: David therefore departed thence, and escaped to the cave Adullam: and when his brethren and all his father's house heard it, they went down thither to him.

And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him; and he became a captain over them: and there were with him about four hundred men. was in debt: Heb. had a creditor discontented: Heb. bitter of soul

waypoints.placeNote: A walled harvest town with gates and bars, near the Philistine border
waypoints.narration: Six miles south along the ridge road stands a walled town, its threshingfloors heaped with the barley harvest. Philistine raiders are stripping the floors. David asks the LORD, twice, and both times the answer is go. His four hundred fall on the raiders, drive off their cattle, and save the town. But walls that keep raiders out can shut a fugitive in. Saul is already marching, and Keilah's grateful elders would still hand David over. He slips out through the gate and turns toward the dry country.
verses: Then they told David, saying, Behold, the Philistines fight against Keilah, and they rob the threshingfloors.
Therefore David enquired of the LORD, saying, Shall I go and smite these Philistines? And the LORD said unto David, Go, and smite the Philistines, and save Keilah.
And David's men said unto him, Behold, we be afraid here in Judah: how much more then if we come to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?
Then David enquired of the LORD yet again. And the LORD answered him and said, Arise, go down to Keilah; for I will deliver the Philistines into thine hand.
So David and his men went to Keilah, and fought with the Philistines, and brought away their cattle, and smote them with a great slaughter. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.

waypoints.placeNote: Dry scrub wilderness in the hill country southeast of Hebron
waypoints.narration: Southeast the land dries out. The wilderness of Ziph is scrub and bare limestone, wadis and strongholds, and Saul hunts it every day. In a wood in that waste Jonathan finds David one last time, the king's son walking out to strengthen the fugitive's hand in God. Fear not, he says; you will be king over Israel, and my father knows it. They cut a covenant between the trees and part. They will not meet again. The Ziphites are already on the road north with David's position.
verses: And David abode in the wilderness in strong holds, and remained in a mountain in the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul sought him every day, but God delivered him not into his hand.
And David saw that Saul was come out to seek his life: and David was in the wilderness of Ziph in a wood.
And Jonathan Saul's son arose, and went to David into the wood, and strengthened his hand in God.
And he said unto him, Fear not: for the hand of Saul my father shall not find thee; and thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee; and that also Saul my father knoweth.
And they two made a covenant before the LORD: and David abode in the wood, and Jonathan went to his house.

waypoints.placeNote: A spring and caves in the cliffs above the Dead Sea
waypoints.narration: The land falls away east, three thousand feet down to the Dead Sea, and at the bottom a spring bursts from the cliff among the rocks of the wild goats. Saul comes hunting with three thousand chosen men and walks alone into the one cave where David's company crouches in the dark. A knife whispers; David cuts the hem of the king's robe and lets him live, and his heart smites him even for the cloth. Saul walks back into the sunlight never knowing how close his death sat.
verses: And it came to pass, when Saul was returned from following the Philistines, that it was told him, saying, Behold, David is in the wilderness of Engedi. following: Heb. after
Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel, and went to seek David and his men upon the rocks of the wild goats.
And he came to the sheepcotes by the way, where was a cave; and Saul went in to cover his feet: and David and his men remained in the sides of the cave.

And the men of David said unto him, Behold the day of which the LORD said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand, that thou mayest do to him as it shall seem good unto thee. Then David arose, and cut off the skirt of Saul's robe privily. Saul's...: Heb. the robe which was Saul's
And it came to pass afterward, that David's heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt.
And he said unto his men, The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD'S anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the anointed of the LORD.
So David stayed his servants with these words, and suffered them not to rise against Saul. But Saul rose up out of the cave, and went on his way. stayed: Heb. cut off

waypoints.placeNote: A Negev border town granted to David by Achish of Gath
waypoints.narration: Long miles southwest through the Negev, past the last wells, to a mud-brick town Achish granted his tame outlaw. David rides home on the third day and finds smoke. Amalekites have burned Ziklag and carried off every wife and child, his own included. The men who followed him through every wilderness now talk of stoning him. Alone at the bottom, David encourages himself in the LORD his God, then musters, pursues, and takes everything back. Days later word comes down from the north: Saul is dead on Gilboa.
verses: And it came to pass, when David and his men were come to Ziklag on the third day, that the Amalekites had invaded the south, and Ziklag, and smitten Ziklag, and burned it with fire;
And had taken the women captives, that were therein: they slew not any, either great or small, but carried them away, and went on their way.
So David and his men came to the city, and, behold, it was burned with fire; and their wives, and their sons, and their daughters, were taken captives.
Then David and the people that were with him lifted up their voice and wept, until they had no more power to weep.
And David's two wives were taken captives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.

And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God. grieved: Heb. bitter

waypoints.placeNote: High city of the patriarchs, where Judah crowned its king
waypoints.narration: The road back climbs northeast out of the Negev into high vineyard country where Abraham once pitched under the oaks. David asks the LORD whether to go up, and the answer names Hebron. He comes with his wives, his men, and their households, and settles into the old city of the patriarchs. There the men of Judah gather and pour oil over the head Saul hunted for seven years. The fugitive road ends at three thousand feet with a crown. The kingdom starts here, uphill from a cave.
verses: And it came to pass after this, that David enquired of the LORD, saying, Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah? And the LORD said unto him, Go up. And David said, Whither shall I go up? And he said, Unto Hebron.
So David went up thither, and his two wives also, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail Nabal's wife the Carmelite.
And his men that were with him did David bring up, every man with his household: and they dwelt in the cities of Hebron.
And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. And they told David, saying, That the men of Jabeshgilead were they that buried Saul.

journeys.title: There and Back
journeys.subtitle: Out by the north road in chains; home to build again
journeys.essay: This is the one journey Israel makes in chains. The prophets had said the road was coming, that Jerusalem's kings had spent the patience of the LORD and Babylon would collect. The wall breaks, the temple burns, and the survivors walk the long arc north and east: up past Riblah, over the Euphrates at Carchemish, then down the river roads to the greatest city on earth. Seventy years the exiles wait there, singing Zion's laments by the canals while Daniel keeps faith inside the palace itself. Then the empire changes hands overnight, and a Persian decree opens the road home. The return is slow and stubborn: an altar first, then a temple, then, generations later, Nehemiah's wall going up in fifty-two days with a trowel in one hand and a spear in the other. The road out measures what rebellion costs. The road back measures what God does not abandon.

waypoints.placeNote: The city of David under Babylonian siege, ninth year of Zedekiah
waypoints.narration: Begin on the wall, tenth month, ninth year of Zedekiah. Nebuchadnezzar's siege forts ring the city, and for the better part of two years nothing comes in. By the fourth month there is no bread left in Jerusalem. Then the wall gives way. The men of war bolt at night through the gate between the two walls by the king's garden, and Zedekiah runs for the Jordan plain. The Chaldeans pour through the breach. Behind you the temple will burn; ahead lies the longest road Judah has ever walked.
verses: And it came to pass in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he, and all his host, against Jerusalem, and pitched against it; and they built forts against it round about.
And the city was besieged unto the eleventh year of king Zedekiah.
And on the ninth day of the fourth month the famine prevailed in the city, and there was no bread for the people of the land.

And the city was broken up, and all the men of war fled by night by the way of the gate between two walls, which is by the king's garden: (now the Chaldees were against the city round about:) and the king went the way toward the plain.

waypoints.placeNote: Babylonian army headquarters on the Orontes, in the land of Hamath
waypoints.narration: The captive king is run down in the plains of Jericho, his army scattered, then marched north two hundred thirty miles up the rift valley and through the Beqaa to a garrison town on the Orontes where Nebuchadnezzar keeps his field headquarters. Judgment is spoken at Riblah. Zedekiah's sons are killed before his eyes; then his eyes are put out, so the last thing the last king of Judah sees is his line ending. Bound in brass, he is carried on toward Babylon. The exiles' column forms on the same road.
verses: And the army of the Chaldees pursued after the king, and overtook him in the plains of Jericho: and all his army were scattered from him.
So they took the king, and brought him up to the king of Babylon to Riblah; and they gave judgment upon him. gave...: Heb. spake judgment with him
And they slew the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him with fetters of brass, and carried him to Babylon. put...: Heb. made blind

waypoints.placeNote: The great Euphrates ford where Babylon broke Egypt's army
waypoints.narration: The road bends east to the great ford of the Euphrates. Here, a generation before the exiles pass, Nebuchadnezzar broke the army of Pharaoh Necho, the battle Jeremiah saw: order the buckler and shield, harness the horses, and then the mighty stumbling and falling toward the north by the river. Carchemish decided who would own Judah, and the chains shuffling past its walls are the long echo of that day. From the crossing, the caravan track follows the river southeast into flat brown country with no hills at all.
verses: Against Egypt, against the army of Pharaohnecho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah.
Order ye the buckler and shield, and draw near to battle.
Harness the horses; and get up, ye horsemen, and stand forth with your helmets; furbish the spears, and put on the brigandines.

Wherefore have I seen them dismayed and turned away back? and their mighty ones are beaten down, and are fled apace, and look not back: for fear was round about, saith the LORD. beaten...: Heb. broken in pieces fled...: Heb. fled a flight
Let not the swift flee away, nor the mighty man escape; they shall stumble, and fall toward the north by the river Euphrates.

waypoints.placeNote: Nebuchadnezzar's capital on the Euphrates, greatest city of the age
waypoints.narration: Weeks along the river, and then the walls: blue-glazed brick, gates of bronze, a ziggurat standing over the flat land, the Euphrates running through the middle of the city. Into this machine the exiles are fed. The king's officers pick through the young men of Judah for the palace schools, and four of them, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, are handed Babylonian names, Babylonian food, and the learning of the Chaldeans. Names can be assigned. What these four keep, in the heart of the empire that burned their city, cannot.
verses: And the king spake unto Ashpenaz the master of his eunuchs, that he should bring certain of the children of Israel, and of the king's seed, and of the princes;

Children in whom was no blemish, but well favoured, and skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science, and such as had ability in them to stand in the king's palace, and whom they might teach the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans.

And the king appointed them a daily provision of the king's meat, and of the wine which he drank: so nourishing them three years, that at the end thereof they might stand before the king. the wine...: Heb. the wine of his drink
Now among these were of the children of Judah, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah:
Unto whom the prince of the eunuchs gave names: for he gave unto Daniel the name of Belteshazzar; and to Hananiah, of Shadrach; and to Mishael, of Meshach; and to Azariah, of Abednego.

waypoints.placeNote: Canal country outside the walls, where the exiles settled and mourned
waypoints.narration: Outside the walls the land is laced with canals, slow brown water under willows, and the settlements of the deported are strung along the banks. Here the songs of Zion turn to laments. How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people. Judah dwells among the heathen and finds no rest; the ways of Zion mourn because none come to the feasts. Seventy years are measured out in this flat green country, planting gardens, raising children, remembering a burned city three months' walk to the west.
verses: How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary!
She weepeth sore in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks: among all her lovers she hath none to comfort her: all her friends have dealt treacherously with her, they are become her enemies.

Judah is gone into captivity because of affliction, and because of great servitude: she dwelleth among the heathen, she findeth no rest: all her persecutors overtook her between the straits. because of great...: Heb. for the greatness of servitude
The ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts: all her gates are desolate: her priests sigh, her virgins are afflicted, and she is in bitterness.

waypoints.placeNote: Persian Babylon in the first year of Cyrus, where the decree went out
waypoints.narration: Empires end. Babylon falls to the Medes and Persians without losing a brick, and in the first year of Cyrus the LORD stirs the new king's spirit. A proclamation goes out in writing through all his kingdom: who is there among you of all his people? Let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD God of Israel.
