Neighbors load the pilgrims with silver and gold, goods and beasts. Thousands of families form up at the western gates, facing home.
verses: Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing, saying, made...: Heb. caused a voice to pass
Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, The LORD God of heaven hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he hath charged me to build him an house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah.

Who is there among you of all his people? his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD God of Israel, (he is the God,) which is in Jerusalem.

And whosoever remaineth in any place where he sojourneth, let the men of his place help him with silver, and with gold, and with goods, and with beasts, beside the freewill offering for the house of God that is in Jerusalem. help...: Heb. lift him up

waypoints.placeNote: Broken walls and burned gates, generations after the fall
waypoints.narration: Four months on the desert road, the last stretch running straight for the hills of home, and what waits at the end is rubble. Years after the first return, Nehemiah arrives, rests three days, then rides out alone at night from the valley gate: past the dragon well, the dung port, the fountain gate, the king's pool, picking through stones where his beast cannot pass. He tells no one what God has put in his heart. By morning he knows every broken course of the wall, and he means to raise it.
verses: So I came to Jerusalem, and was there three days.
And I arose in the night, I and some few men with me; neither told I any man what my God had put in my heart to do at Jerusalem: neither was there any beast with me, save the beast that I rode upon.

And I went out by night by the gate of the valley, even before the dragon well, and to the dung port, and viewed the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down, and the gates thereof were consumed with fire.
Then I went on to the gate of the fountain, and to the king's pool: but there was no place for the beast that was under me to pass.
Then went I up in the night by the brook, and viewed the wall, and turned back, and entered by the gate of the valley, and so returned.

waypoints.placeNote: Jerusalem's rebuilt circuit, closed in fifty-two days
waypoints.narration: Fifty-two days. Half the workers build with one hand and hold a weapon with the other; the courses climb out of the rubble notch by notch, gate by gate, while enemies jeer that a fox could break it down. On the twenty-fifth of Elul the last gap closes and the circuit stands whole. The nations round about are cast down in their own eyes, for they perceive this work was wrought of God. The road out took chains and three months. The road home took ninety years, and it ends on a wall.
verses: So the wall was finished in the twenty and fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty and two days.

And it came to pass, that when all our enemies heard thereof, and all the heathen that were about us saw these things, they were much cast down in their own eyes: for they perceived that this work was wrought of our God.

journeys.title: The Galilee Road
journeys.subtitle: From a hill town to an empty tomb
journeys.essay: Nearly every mile of this road can still be walked. It begins in a hill town too small for the maps and ends at the most contested gates on earth. Between them lie the brown water of the Jordan, the badlands where hunger was answered with scripture, a wedding at Cana, and the lake — always the lake — with its fishing towns, sudden storms, and borrowed boats. Jesus worked mostly within thirty miles of Capernaum, yet the road kept pulling at the edges: north to the pagan springs of Caesarea Philippi, where Peter said out loud who he was, then south, down the rift valley to Jericho and up the long climb to Jerusalem. The Gospels are walking documents; distances and place names carry real weight in them. Follow the places in order and the shape appears — a widening circuit around Galilee, then one deliberate, unhurried march toward a city that would kill him, and a tomb that could not hold him.

waypoints.placeNote: Hill town of Jesus' boyhood, overlooking the Jezreel plain
waypoints.narration: A ridge town in lower Galilee, terraced with olives, looking south over the Jezreel plain. The street climbs past cisterns and flat-roofed stone houses to a small synagogue. Jesus grew up here, a carpenter's son among carpenters. On a sabbath he stands up to read, unrolls Isaiah, and finds the lines about good news for the poor and sight for the blind. He rolls the scroll shut, sits down, and says the words are fulfilled today. The town that raised him will try to throw him off its own cliff. The road starts downhill.
verses: And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read.
And there was delivered unto him the book of the prophet Esaias. And when he had opened the book, he found the place where it was written,

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,
To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.
And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him.
And he began to say unto them, This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.

waypoints.placeNote: Fords of the Jordan near Jericho, where John baptized
waypoints.narration: Down off the ridge, east across the plain, then the long descent of the Jordan valley — sixty miles of heat, tamarisk thickets, and river smell. At the fords near Jericho, John is baptizing crowds in slow brown water. Jesus walks in from Galilee like any other traveler and steps into the current. John balks; Jesus insists. When he comes up out of the water the sky opens, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and a voice from heaven names him the beloved Son. The road has found its walker.
verses: Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him.
But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?
And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him.
And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:
And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.

waypoints.placeNote: Judean badlands west of the Jordan, forty days of fasting
waypoints.narration: West of the river the land breaks into badlands — chalk hills, dry wadis, no shade, no bread. Jesus goes up into this country alone and fasts forty days. The tempter comes when hunger is loudest: stones into bread, a leap from the temple pinnacle, all the kingdoms of the world for one bow. Each time Jesus answers with a written word and nothing else, and the third answer is a dismissal. The wild country keeps its silence; the angels come after. A man who will feed thousands first learns to be hungry.
verses: Then was Jesus led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil.
And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred.
And when the tempter came to him, he said, If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread.
But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple,

And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.
Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. tempt: or, try, or, put to trial, or, proof
Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them;
And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me.
Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.

waypoints.placeNote: Galilee village north of Nazareth, site of the first sign
waypoints.narration: Back up the valley and into the Galilee hills, to a village a few miles north of Nazareth. A wedding is running long and the wine has run out — a small disaster in a small town, the kind neighbors remember for years. Six stone waterpots stand by the door for the washing rites. Jesus has them filled to the brim, then drawn and carried to the master of the feast, who tastes the best wine of the day and cannot say where it came from. The first sign, done quietly, at somebody else's party.
verses: And there were set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece.
Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim.
And he saith unto them, Draw out now, and bear unto the governor of the feast. And they bare it.
When the ruler of the feast had tasted the water that was made wine, and knew not whence it was: (but the servants which drew the water knew;) the governor of the feast called the bridegroom,
And saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now.
This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him.

waypoints.placeNote: Fishing town on the lake's north shore, Jesus' base camp
waypoints.narration: Down to the lakeshore, where Capernaum sits on the north rim of the Sea of Galilee — black basalt houses, boats drawn up on the shingle, a customs post on the highway to Damascus. This becomes the base camp for everything that follows. On the sabbath Jesus teaches in the synagogue and the room goes still: he speaks with authority, not citation. A man with an unclean spirit cries out against him, and Jesus silences it with a word. The news runs around the lake faster than any boat.
verses: And they went into Capernaum; and straightway on the sabbath day he entered into the synagogue, and taught.
And they were astonished at his doctrine: for he taught them as one that had authority, and not as the scribes.
And there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit; and he cried out,
Saying, Let us alone; what have we to do with thee, thou Jesus of Nazareth? art thou come to destroy us? I know thee who thou art, the Holy One of God.
And Jesus rebuked him, saying, Hold thy peace, and come out of him.
And when the unclean spirit had torn him, and cried with a loud voice, he came out of him.

And they were all amazed, insomuch that they questioned among themselves, saying, What thing is this? what new doctrine is this? for with authority commandeth he even the unclean spirits, and they do obey him.

waypoints.placeNote: Open water of the Sea of Galilee, mid-crossing at night
waypoints.narration: Evening on the lake. The boats push off for the far side, Jesus asleep on a cushion in the stern. The Sea of Galilee lies in a bowl seven hundred feet below the ocean, and wind funnels down the gorges without warning. A squall drops, waves break over the gunwale, the ship begins to fill. The fishermen — men who have worked this water all their lives — wake him in a panic. He rebukes the wind, tells the sea to be still, and the calm that follows is heavier than the storm was.
verses: And the same day, when the even was come, he saith unto them, Let us pass over unto the other side.
And when they had sent away the multitude, they took him even as he was in the ship. And there were also with him other little ships.
And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full.
And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish?
And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
And they feared exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

waypoints.placeNote: Fishing village at the upper Jordan's mouth, home of Peter and Andrew
waypoints.narration: Landfall near the mouth of the upper Jordan, at Bethsaida — hometown of Peter, Andrew, and Philip, a fishing village grown into a Greek-styled town. They bring a blind man and beg for a touch. Jesus takes him by the hand and leads him out of the town, away from the crowd. The healing comes in stages: first men like walking trees, then every man clearly. It is the only cure in the Gospels told in two touches, done on a roadside and sent home quietly. Sight, like the road, comes a stretch at a time.
verses: And he cometh to Bethsaida; and they bring a blind man unto him, and besought him to touch him.
And he took the blind man by the hand, and led him out of the town; and when he had spit on his eyes, and put his hands upon him, he asked him if he saw ought.
And he looked up, and said, I see men as trees, walking.
After that he put his hands again upon his eyes, and made him look up: and he was restored, and saw every man clearly.
And he sent him away to his house, saying, Neither go into the town, nor tell it to any in the town.

waypoints.placeNote: Pagan spring city under Mount Hermon, at the Jordan's headwaters
waypoints.narration: North up the Jordan's headwaters to the springs under Mount Hermon, where snowmelt pours from a cliff at a shrine to Pan — Roman marble, carved niches, cold water. In the shadow of every god the empire keeps, Jesus asks the walking question: who do men say that I am. Then, closer: but who do you say. Peter answers — the Christ, the Son of the living God — and Jesus calls him blessed, for flesh and blood did not reveal it. This is the road's northern limit. From here the way turns south, toward Jerusalem.
verses: When Jesus came into the coasts of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying, Whom do men say that I the Son of man am?
And they said, Some say that thou art John the Baptist: some, Elias; and others, Jeremias, or one of the prophets.
He saith unto them, But whom say ye that I am?
And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.
And Jesus answered and said unto him, Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven.

waypoints.placeNote: Palm city in the rift valley, the lowest town on earth
waypoints.narration: The long road south again, the whole length of the Jordan valley down to Jericho — palm groves, balsam trade, tax money, the lowest town on earth. Crowds pack the street for the passing rabbi. A short rich man named Zacchaeus, chief among the publicans, climbs a sycomore tree to see over the heads. Jesus stops under the branches, calls him down by name, and invites himself to the most hated house in town. By dinner, half of Zacchaeus's goods belong to the poor. Salvation, Jesus says, has come to this house today.
verses: And Jesus entered and passed through Jericho.
And, behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, which was the chief among the publicans, and he was rich.
And he sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature.
And he ran before, and climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way.
And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house.
And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully.
And when they saw it, they all murmured, saying, That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner.
And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.
And Jesus said unto him, This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham.

waypoints.placeNote: Ridge east of Jerusalem, above Bethphage and Bethany
waypoints.narration: The climb out of the rift is the hardest walking on the road — three thousand feet gained through bare rock from Jericho toward the city. It tops out on the Mount of Olives, at Bethphage and Bethany, with Jerusalem suddenly filling the view across the Kidron valley. Jesus sends two disciples ahead for a colt that has never been ridden. They throw their cloaks over it; he rides. The pilgrim crowd spreads garments and cut branches on the road and shouts Hosanna. The city gates stand open. The last miles are downhill.
verses: And when they came nigh to Jerusalem, unto Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount of Olives, he sendeth forth two of his disciples,
And saith unto them, Go your way into the village over against you: and as soon as ye be entered into it, ye shall find a colt tied, whereon never man sat; loose him, and bring him.
And if any man say unto you, Why do ye this? say ye that the Lord hath need of him; and straightway he will send him hither.
And they went their way, and found the colt tied by the door without in a place where two ways met; and they loose him.
And certain of them that stood there said unto them, What do ye, loosing the colt?
And they said unto them even as Jesus had commanded: and they let them go.
And they brought the colt to Jesus, and cast their garments on him; and he sat upon him.
And many spread their garments in the way: and others cut down branches off the trees, and strawed them in the way.
And they that went before, and they that followed, cried, saying, Hosanna; Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord:
Blessed be the kingdom of our father David, that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest.

waypoints.placeNote: The holy city at Passover, cross and empty tomb
waypoints.narration: Across the Kidron and through the gate: Jerusalem at Passover, the end of every road in this story. Here came the last supper, the arrest under the olive trees, the trials, and a crucifixion outside the wall. The journey does not stop at the cross. Before dawn on the first day of the week, women carry spices to a rock-cut tomb and find the stone rolled aside and the body gone. Two men in shining garments ask why they seek the living among the dead. He is risen. The road goes on from here.
verses: Now upon the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they came unto the sepulchre, bringing the spices which they had prepared, and certain others with them.
And they found the stone rolled away from the sepulchre.
And they entered in, and found not the body of the Lord Jesus.
And it came to pass, as they were much perplexed thereabout, behold, two men stood by them in shining garments:
And as they were afraid, and bowed down their faces to the earth, they said unto them, Why seek ye the living among the dead? the living: or, him that liveth
He is not here, but is risen: remember how he spake unto you when he was yet in Galilee,
Saying, The Son of man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and the third day rise again.

journeys.title: The Wayfaring Apostle
journeys.subtitle: One man's roads and sea lanes across the empire
journeys.essay: Saul of Tarsus was knocked down on one road and spent the rest of his life on all the others. This journey stitches his travels into a single line: from the Damascus road, through Antioch — the sending city — out across Cyprus and the highlands of Asia Minor, over the Aegean to Macedonia and Greece, and back through Ephesus toward the arrest in Jerusalem. Acts is a book of harbors and mile markers; Luke counts the days at sea and names the winds. Paul moved the way the empire moved — Roman roads, grain ships, garrison towns — and used every mile of it to plant churches he would later write to from prison. The line ends in Rome, not in triumph but under guard, in a rented house with an open door. By then the word had crossed from a Jewish province to the capital of the world, carried the whole way at walking pace and sail speed.

waypoints.placeNote: Highway north from Jerusalem, near the gates of Damascus
waypoints.narration: The high road from Jerusalem to Damascus, six days' travel through dry country, with the city's orchards finally green on the horizon. Saul of Tarsus rides it carrying letters from the high priest — warrants for arrests. Near the gates, light out of heaven drops him to the ground and a voice calls his name twice: Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me. He asks who is speaking and gets the answer that unmakes him — I am Jesus. Blind, led by the hand, he enters Damascus a different man. Every mile after this one belongs to that voice.
verses: And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,
And desired of him letters to Damascus to the synagogues, that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem. of this way: Gr. of the way
And as he journeyed, he came near Damascus: and suddenly there shined round about him a light from heaven:
And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?
And he said, Who art thou, Lord? And the Lord said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.
And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do.

waypoints.placeNote: Syrian metropolis on the Orontes, the first sending church
waypoints.narration: North through Syria to Antioch on the Orontes, third city of the empire — half a million people, colonnaded streets, every god for sale. Greeks here are turning to the Lord by the hundreds, and Jerusalem sends Barnabas to see it. Barnabas sees the grace of God, is glad, and walks to Tarsus to hunt up Saul. For a whole year the two of them teach the crowds in this pagan city, and here the nickname sticks: Christians. Antioch, not Jerusalem, will be the port every missionary road leaves from.
verses: Then tidings of these things came unto the ears of the church which was in Jerusalem: and they sent forth Barnabas, that he should go as far as Antioch.
Who, when he came, and had seen the grace of God, was glad, and exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord.
For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Ghost and of faith: and much people was added unto the Lord.
Then departed Barnabas to Tarsus, for to seek Saul:

And when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch. with...: or, in the church

waypoints.placeNote: Roman capital of Cyprus, seat of the proconsul
waypoints.narration: Down to the harbor at Seleucia and out to sea for the first time — to Cyprus, Barnabas's home island, then the length of it on foot to Paphos, the Roman capital on the western shore. The deputy Sergius Paulus, a prudent man, asks to hear the word of God; his court sorcerer Elymas works to turn him from it. Saul — using the Roman name Paul now — fixes his eyes on the magician and calls blindness down on him: a mist, a darkness, a groping for hands to lead him. The deputy believes, astonished. The first governor has come over.
verses: And when they had gone through the isle unto Paphos, they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Barjesus:
Which was with the deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man; who called for Barnabas and Saul, and desired to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the sorcerer (for so is his name by interpretation) withstood them, seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith.
Then Saul, (who also is called Paul,) filled with the Holy Ghost, set his eyes on him,
And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon thee, and thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season. And immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness; and he went about seeking some to lead him by the hand.
Then the deputy, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord.

waypoints.placeNote: Garrison town on the cold Lycaonian plain
waypoints.narration: Over the sea to Pamphylia, then up rough passes into the Lycaonian uplands — Lystra, a Roman garrison town on a windswept plain. A man lame from his mother's womb listens to Paul, who sees faith in him and tells him to stand upright. He leaps and walks. The town decides the gods have come down: Barnabas is Jupiter, Paul is Mercurius, and the priest brings oxen and garlands to the gates for sacrifice. The apostles tear their clothes and run into the crowd to stop it. Later the same crowd will stone Paul and drag him out for dead. He gets up.
verses: And there sat a certain man at Lystra, impotent in his feet, being a cripple from his mother's womb, who never had walked:
The same heard Paul speak: who stedfastly beholding him, and perceiving that he had faith to be healed,
Said with a loud voice, Stand upright on thy feet. And he leaped and walked.
And when the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men.
And they called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius, because he was the chief speaker.
Then the priest of Jupiter, which was before their city, brought oxen and garlands unto the gates, and would have done sacrifice with the people.
Which when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of, they rent their clothes, and ran in among the people, crying out,

And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:

waypoints.placeNote: Aegean port near old Troy, where Asia runs out
waypoints.narration: West across Asia Minor with a strange wind against every plan — forbidden to preach in Asia, blocked from Bithynia — until the land itself runs out at Troas, a harbor town near the ruins of Troy, with Europe a gray line across the water. In the night a vision stands over Paul: a man of Macedonia, pleading, come over into Macedonia and help us. In the morning the company looks for a ship. This is the hinge of the whole map — the word about to cross from Asia into Europe on the strength of a dream.
verses: And they passing by Mysia came down to Troas.
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them.

waypoints.placeNote: Roman colony in Macedonia on the Egnatian Way
waypoints.narration: Two days' sail past Samothrace to Neapolis, then up the paved Egnatian Way to Philippi, a Roman colony proud of its citizenship. Preaching gets Paul and Silas stripped, beaten with rods, and locked in the inner prison with their feet in the stocks. At midnight they pray and sing, and the prisoners listen. An earthquake shakes the foundations, every door open, every chain loose. The jailer draws his sword, sure his prisoners are gone; Paul calls out of the dark, we are all here. Before sunrise the jailer washes their wounds and asks what he must do to be saved.
verses: And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one's bands were loosed.
And the keeper of the prison awaking out of his sleep, and seeing the prison doors open, he drew out his sword, and would have killed himself, supposing that the prisoners had been fled.
But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, Do thyself no harm: for we are all here.
Then he called for a light, and sprang in, and came trembling, and fell down before Paul and Silas,
And brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved?
And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house.

waypoints.placeNote: City of philosophers and idols, home of Mars' hill
waypoints.narration: South by road and sea to Athens — marble, philosophy, and more idols than men, as the old joke ran. Paul walks the city with his spirit stirred, argues in the market with Stoics and Epicureans, and is brought up onto Mars' hill to explain his strange doctrine. He starts from their own altar, inscribed TO THE UNKNOWN GOD, and declares the God who made the world and everything in it, who dwells in no temple made with hands — in whom we live, and move, and have our being. Some mock. A few climb down the hill with him.
verses: Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious. Mars' hill: or, the court of the Areopagites

For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you. devotions: or, gods that ye worship
God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands;
Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things;
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us:
For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.

waypoints.placeNote: Two-harbored boomtown on the isthmus of Greece
waypoints.narration: A short road west along the gulf to Corinth, the boomtown on the isthmus — two harbors, sailors' wages, a rough reputation. Paul works leather and canvas with Aquila and Priscilla, tentmakers like himself, and reasons in the synagogue every sabbath. When the opposition turns to blasphemy he shakes out his raiment and moves next door, to the house of Justus, and the ruler of the synagogue follows him there. In the night the Lord speaks by vision: be not afraid, I have much people in this city. He stays a year and six months.
verses: And when Silas and Timotheus were come from Macedonia, Paul was pressed in the spirit, and testified to the Jews that Jesus was Christ. was Christ: or, is the Christ
And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean: from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.
And he departed thence, and entered into a certain man's house, named Justus, one that worshipped God, whose house joined hard to the synagogue.
And Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue, believed on the Lord with all his house; and many of the Corinthians hearing believed, and were baptized.
Then spake the Lord to Paul in the night by a vision, Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace:
For I am with thee, and no man shall set on thee to hurt thee: for I have much people in this city.
And he continued there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. continued there: Gr. sat there

waypoints.placeNote: Warden city of the temple of Diana
waypoints.narration: Across the Aegean to Ephesus, keeper of the temple of Diana, one of the wonders of the world. Paul stays longer here than anywhere — years of daily teaching — until the idol business feels it in the ledger. Demetrius the silversmith, who makes silver shrines for the goddess, calls the craftsmen together: this Paul says gods made with hands are no gods at all, and our craft is in danger. The city packs the great theater and chants with one voice, great is Diana of the Ephesians. The gospel has grown big enough to start a riot.
verses: And the same time there arose no small stir about that way.
For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen;
Whom he called together with the workmen of like occupation, and said, Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth.
Moreover ye see and hear, that not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods, which are made with hands:

So that not only this our craft is in danger to be set at nought; but also that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worshippeth. set at nought: or, brought into disrepute, or, contempt
And when they heard these sayings, they were full of wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians.

waypoints.placeNote: The temple city, where the mob and the chains waited
waypoints.narration: The long sea road home — Miletus, Rhodes, Tyre, Caesarea — with prophets at every port saying that chains wait in Jerusalem. Paul goes anyway. In the temple courts a rumor flares that he has brought Greeks past the barrier, and the whole city moves at once: doors slammed, Paul dragged out, fists falling. Roman soldiers run down from the fortress stairs and pull him from the mob, bind him with two chains, and carry him up bodily while the crowd surges behind, crying, away with him. The prisoner years begin here.
verses: And all the city was moved, and the people ran together: and they took Paul, and drew him out of the temple: and forthwith the doors were shut.
And as they went about to kill him, tidings came unto the chief captain of the band, that all Jerusalem was in an uproar.
Who immediately took soldiers and centurions, and ran down unto them: and when they saw the chief captain and the soldiers, they left beating of Paul.
Then the chief captain came near, and took him, and commanded him to be bound with two chains; and demanded who he was, and what he had done.
And some cried one thing, some another, among the multitude: and when he could not know the certainty for the tumult, he commanded him to be carried into the castle.
And when he came upon the stairs, so it was, that he was borne of the soldiers for the violence of the people.
For the multitude of the people followed after, crying, Away with him.

waypoints.placeNote: Open sea off Crete, fourteen days adrift
waypoints.narration: A grain ship out of Alexandria, two hundred seventy-six souls aboard, beating west too late in the sailing season. Off Crete a tempestuous northeaster — Euroclydon — takes the ship and will not give it back. The crew frap the hull with cables, throw the cargo overboard, then the tackle with their own hands, and drive under bare poles day after day. No sun, no stars, no reckoning; all hope of being saved is taken away. Paul, the prisoner, stands up in the waist of the ship and tells them God has granted him every life aboard.
verses: But not long after there arose against it a tempestuous wind, called Euroclydon. arose: or, beat
And when the ship was caught, and could not bear up into the wind, we let her drive.
And running under a certain island which is called Clauda, we had much work to come by the boat:
Which when they had taken up, they used helps, undergirding the ship; and, fearing lest they should fall into the quicksands, strake sail, and so were driven.
And we being exceedingly tossed with a tempest, the next day they lightened the ship;
And the third day we cast out with our own hands the tackling of the ship.
And when neither sun nor stars in many days appeared, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope that we should be saved was then taken away.

waypoints.placeNote: The island of Melita, landfall after shipwreck
waypoints.narration: Soundings shoal in the dark; four anchors go down off an unknown coast. At daylight they run the ship aground in a bay, and every soul comes ashore through the surf — swimming, or riding planks and broken timber — onto the island called Melita. The islanders kindle a fire in the rain and the cold. A viper strikes out of the gathered sticks and fastens on Paul's hand; he shakes it into the flames and stands there unharmed while the crowd waits for him to swell and fall dead. They decide he is a god. Three months of winter follow.
verses: And when they were escaped, then they knew that the island was called Melita.
And the barbarous people shewed us no little kindness: for they kindled a fire, and received us every one, because of the present rain, and because of the cold.
And when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks, and laid them on the fire, there came a viper out of the heat, and fastened on his hand.

And when the barbarians saw the venomous beast hang on his hand, they said among themselves, No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he hath escaped the sea, yet vengeance suffereth not to live.
And he shook off the beast into the fire, and felt no harm.

Howbeit they looked when he should have swollen, or fallen down dead suddenly: but after they had looked a great while, and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds, and said that he was a god.

waypoints.placeNote: Capital of the empire, end of the road
waypoints.narration: Spring, and a ship of Alexandria with the Twin Brothers for a figurehead — Syracuse, Rhegium, Puteoli, then the Appian Way north on foot. Believers walk out from the city as far as the Three Taverns to meet him, and Paul thanks God and takes courage. In Rome he lives two whole years in his own hired house, a soldier chained at his wrist, receiving all who come, preaching the kingdom of God with all confidence, no man forbidding him. The road that began with a blinding light ends at the center of the world, still open.
verses: Be it known therefore unto you, that the salvation of God is sent unto the Gentiles, and that they will hear it.
And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, and had great reasoning among themselves.
And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him,
Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him.
